Twenty Third Indian Antarctic Expedition 2003 -2005
Ministry of Earth Sciences, Technical Publication No. 21, pp 105-112
Geomagnetic and Atmospheric Electrical 
Parameter Variations observed at Maitri, Antarctica
C. Panneerselvam, P. Elango, C. P. Anil Kumar, K. U. Nair, K. Jeeva,
C. Selvaraj, S. Gurubaran, Ajay Dhar and B. M. Pathan
Indian Institute of Geomagnetism 
Plot 5, Sector 18, New Panvel (W), Navi Mumbai
ABSTRACT
Surface m easurem ents of the atm ospheric electrical param eters, viz. 
ionosphere to ground currents, electric field and geomagnetic field were carried 
out at the Indian station, Maitri (Geog. 70.75° S, 11.75°E, 117 m above mean sea 
level), Antarctica. The averaged pattern of diurnal variations in the electric field 
and Maxwell current density averaged over selected fair weather days nearly follows 
the Carnegie curve, with a minimum around 0300 UT and a maximum around 1900 
UT. However during magnetically disturbed days, there is a departure from universal 
diurnal variation in both the electric field and vertical conduction current, which is 
attributed to the influence of solar wind-magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling. 
Examining the cause in detail will require further investigation. The correlation 
coefficient between the current and electric field had a high value (more than 0.75) 
for all these days. The measured atmospheric electric field and geomagnetic field 
variations were compared. The experimental data used for the analysis were of 2004 
and 2005. The mean daily variation of atmospheric electric field and the horizontal 
magnetic components showed a coincidence for the selected fair weather days 
during magnetic quiet days. Some examples are presented in this paper. Further 
measurements and studies involving statistical analysis are needed. This study 
will help us to examine the impact of upper atmospheric contribution to the geo­
electrical parameters during different geomagnetic conditions.
INTRODUCTION
Wilson (1925) suggested that, the worldwide thunderstorm activity 
maintains the global electric potential between the ionosphere and the Earth’s 
surface. Tropical thunder- storms are considered as a main source of electric 
field in the lower atmosphere, drawing current upward to the ionosphere. In 
this way, the global thunderstorm activity is able to maintain a time varying 
electric potential difference of -300 kV, directed downward between the

equipotent surfaces of the ionosphere and the ground in fair-weather regions 
(Adlerman et al., 1996). The atmospheric vertical electric field, conductivity 
and total current density are the three closely related parameters of the 
atmospheric electricity that are required to be observed for obtaining an adequate 
description of the fair-weather atmospheric electric circuit (Israel, 1973).
The Global Electric Circuit (GEC) links the lower atmosphere with 
the ionosphere and the magnetosphere. Measurement of atmospheric electrical 
parameters is handy for investigating the linkage between these regions. 
Long-term measurements would be considered useful for addressing some 
of the problems associated with global change. The measuring site needs to 
be free of atmospheric aerosols and convective activity, because they obscure 
the weak signatures representing the global thunderstorm activity (Israel, 
1973). Measurements from Antarctica will allow us to investigate global 
and local components of global electric circuit. The local components, viz. 
blizzard, wind turbulence, snowfall and clouds, generate a significant effect 
on electrical processes and enable us to understand the electrical climate of 
the Antarctic plateau (Byrne et al., 1993).
There is almost no thunderstorm activity at high latitude. Therefore 
atmospheric currents in these regions can be regarded as a closure segment 
of the global electric circuit. The global circuit involves lower atmosphere 
generators and upper atmosphere generators, the latter being significant in 
the polar cap region. The atmospheric electrical measurements made in 
Antarctica are useful in investigating large scale electrical processes unique 
to high altitude (Byrne et al., 1991). The down ward air-earth current being 
delivered to the surface of the Antarctica plateau is larger than the global 
average owing to its high latitude. Because of its orography, Antarctica is 
strongly coupled to the GEC. Secondly, Antarctic plateau supports a desert 
like climate with clear skies and very low atmospheric aerosol content. In 
summer, the prevailing winds are light and flowing in a nearly constant 
direction and the atmosphere is relatively free of turbulent and convective 
motions (Byrne et al., 1993). Thus the wind induced conductivity fluctuations 
that contribute to meteorological noise in the measured atmospheric electric 
parameters are minimized when experiments are conducted in Antarctic. In
